listenings.text: And now the part of the programme where we save you from an awkward moment abroad. Tipping. In Japan, do not do it. Leaving money on the table can be taken as an insult, and staff have been known to run after tourists to give it back. In the United States it is the opposite. Between eighteen and twenty-two per cent is normal, it is not optional in any real sense, and waiters are paid on the assumption that you will leave it. In much of Europe the service is already on the bill, and anything you add is a small round number, not a percentage. Our practical advice is simple. Ask a local, or look at the bottom of the bill before you reach for your wallet, because in a lot of countries you have already paid.

Hello, it is Ana from finance, about the trip. Two things, and then I will leave you alone. First, please keep every receipt, including the small ones. I know it is annoying, and I know a coffee is three euros, but a payment with no paper does not exist as far as we are concerned. Second, there is about a third of the budget left, which is enough if there are no surprises. One more thing, and this is the important one. Try to avoid paying in cash, because that is where the receipts disappear. Card everything, keep the paper, and send it all to me on Friday. Thank you.

extra_audio.text: Grace asks whether they are finished or would like the dessert menu. Janderson says they are finished and asks for the bill. Grace asks whether it is all together or they would like to split it. He says all together, and asks how much the service charge is. Grace answers ten per cent, and says it is already on the bill.

paras: There are three ways a table of eight people can deal with a bill, and every country prefers a different one. One person pays and everybody sends the money later. Everybody pays for exactly what they ate. Or the bill is divided by eight, and the person who had a starter and a coffee quietly pays for somebody else's steak.

The third one is the fastest and the least fair, and it is also the most common, because arguing about eleven euros in front of a waiter costs more than eleven euros in dignity. Most people know this and pay anyway, which is a small daily proof that we do not decide these things with a calculator.

There is also the service charge, which changes everything and which almost nobody checks. In much of Europe it is already on the bill, so the tip you add on top is a small round number and not a percentage. In the United States it is not there at all and the number you add is not optional. In Japan, leaving anything can be taken as an insult.

So the useful habit for a traveller is not generosity. It is looking at the bottom of the bill before reaching for a wallet, and asking one short question when the answer is not printed. How much is the service charge. Five words, and they save you from the two mistakes that people abroad make most often: paying twice, and paying nothing at all.
reading.source: Article -- a travel column in a weekend newspaper
